cards.title: Define a job as progress in a circumstance
cards.summary: Jobs Theory defines the unit of innovation as the progress a person seeks in a specific circumstance, not a product category or customer type.
cards.use_when: When framing a new product, offer or campaign and you need to state clearly what the customer is actually trying to accomplish rather than describing features or audience demographics.
steps: Write the job as a sentence about progress: 'I want to ___ in this situation.' Avoid naming your product or 'I need ___'.

Specify the circumstance: where, when, with whom, while doing what, and what happens before and after. Circumstance is the unit of analysis because the same person wants different things in different situations.
Describe the functional, social and emotional dimensions of the progress. Social and emotional needs can outweigh functional ones (e.g. trusting someone with your children).
Treat the job as ongoing and recurring rather than a single event; people re-hire solutions whenever the circumstance recurs.
Check it is a job, not a 'need' or a life theme. 'I need to eat' and 'I want to be a good dad' are too general to guide a specific product choice.
caveats: A job is discovered, not created; the underlying job endures even as solutions change.
Jobs are fragile, story-like insights: breaking them into binary segments (male/female, new/existing) destroys meaning.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Film the mini-documentary to characterise a job
cards.summary: Five prompts turn a vague customer struggle into a fully specified Job to Be Done by imagining a filmed episode of the customer's struggle.
cards.use_when: When you need to flesh out a job for messaging, product design or an interview guide and the usual demographic or needs-based descriptions feel empty.
steps: State the progress the person is trying to achieve: what would 'better' look like for them.
Capture the circumstances: who, when, where, while doing what. Example from the source: a manager wants their sales force better equipped so churn falls.
List the obstacles in the way: failed attempts, frustrations, dead ends ('I've tried whitening toothpastes and they don't really work').
Identify compensating behaviour: are they using an imperfect product, cobbling together a workaround, or doing nothing? All three are signals of a live job.
Ask how they would define 'quality' in a better solution and which tradeoffs they would accept (e.g. professional-level whitening without the cost and inconvenience of a dentist visit).
caveats: The answers are rich in context and resist spreadsheet breakdown; cluster them into a coherent story rather than segmenting further.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use jobs theory to redraw your competitive landscape
cards.summary: Competition should be defined by everything the customer could hire in the same circumstance, not by products the industry buckets together.
cards.use_when: When assessing competitors, setting positioning, or feeling that your market is a zero-sum fight among near-identical products.
steps: Ask what else the customer could 'hire' to get the same progress in that circumstance, including non-consumption (doing nothing).
Expect non-obvious competitors: Netflix's Reed Hastings said it competes with everything you do to relax, including video games and a bottle of wine.
Look at substitutions across categories: a smoker taking a break for calm, a social moment and a work escape may be served by cigarettes or by Facebook.

Benchmark outside your category once the true job is identified - BMW, after reframing its job as mobility, found itself competing with Tesla, Uber, Zipcar and self-driving projects, and launched BMW i and DriveNow.
Redraw the market size: SNHU's online division was not really fighting local colleges but competing against adults choosing non-consumption, which is a far larger opportunity.
caveats: Working out the true job can take sustained effort and goes against habits built around product-attribute or demographic framing.
Do not assume the new framing makes you win; it only reveals who you must beat.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Diagnose why needs- and trends-based innovation fails
cards.summary: Needs, trends and guiding principles are too general to predict a purchase; jobs are specific enough to build an innovation blueprint.
cards.use_when: When a product or campaign built around an important-sounding need or a trend has stalled, or when reviewing an innovation brief that lacks circumstantial detail.
steps: Check whether your framing is a need ('I need to eat', 'I need personal transportation'), a trend, or a life theme ('I want to be a good dad'). These are directionally useful but cannot tell you what someone will choose or whether they will act at all.
Note that needs don't explain behaviour: people eat when not hungry, skip meals, and act for reasons unrelated to the need.
Replace the general statement with the job: the progress sought in a particular circumstance, with its functional, social and emotional dimensions and the tradeoffs the customer will make.
Use the Segway as a cautionary example: it was built around 'more efficient personal transportation' without answering whose need, when and in what circumstances.
Forecast the conversion effect: a specific job gives you the criteria for what is essential versus extraneous in the offer, while a need does not.
caveats: Needs and trends are not wrong, just insufficient for predicting choice on their own.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Ask 'what has to prove true' before committing resources
cards.summary: Discovery-driven planning forces teams to surface and test the assumptions behind a new initiative before large investment locks them in.
cards.use_when: When approving a new product, channel or market entry, or when projections look attractive but rest on untested beliefs.
steps: Write down every assumption that must be true for the strategy to succeed - the source calls this discovery-driven planning (MacMillan and McGrath).
Rank assumptions by importance and by how uncertain they are.
Test the most critical, least certain assumptions cheaply and early, before assigning significant money, time and headcount.
Do not adjust projections after the fact to match what is actually happening; treat each assumption as something to be proven or falsified.
Watch for the failure pattern: projects get approved on incorrect guesses, the team becomes 100 percent committed, and nobody wants to tell management the original assumptions were wrong.
caveats: The source presents this as a complement to Jobs Theory, not a replacement for having a causal theory of customer choice.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Apply Jobs Theory only where a real struggle exists
cards.summary: Jobs Theory is not universal; it stops being useful when existing solutions are good enough or the decision is purely rational and calculable.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to run a jobs-based research project or whether another method (efficiency analysis, price modelling) is the better tool.
steps: Confirm there is a genuine struggle for progress; if existing solutions are good enough, jobs research has little to explain.

Check whether the purchase decision is largely mathematical, such as commodity trading or straightforward cost and efficiency comparisons; there the source says jobs theory is not useful because there is no complex bundle of social, emotional and functional needs.
Treat theory as if-then propositions: a good theory says when it applies and when it does not, and telling you when it fails is itself valuable.
Use anomalies as opportunities to sharpen the theory rather than discarding it wholesale.
caveats: Cost or efficiency is explicitly not a core element of a job, so don't force a jobs frame onto a purely economic decision.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use theory as a causal lens, not a formula
cards.summary: Good theory tells you how to think about causes and produces if-then predictions you can test, unlike borrowed best practices.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing an innovation problem, teaching a team to reason about customer choice, or when results from industry best practices are inconsistent.
steps: Ask the causal question first: what actually causes a customer to purchase and use this product or service?
Apply a theory like a lens: use it to explain why past problems and opportunities emerged, then to predict what is likely next and what actions will be needed.
Prefer theories that dispense advice as if-then statements over probabilistic tools, hunches or tips that worked for other companies.
Remember Pasteur: identifying the causal mechanism (germs) enabled prevention and vaccines, while correlation (Snow's water pump) only improved the situation without explaining it.
Recognise that theories are not right or wrong but more or less accurate predictions given the circumstances you are in.
caveats: This is a management-practice argument from the source; theory still needs testing and refinement in your own context.
Prioritise different theories by the problem at hand rather than applying jobs theory to everything.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Look outside the four habitual innovation lenses
cards.summary: Most managers organise innovation around product attributes, customer characteristics, trends or competitive response - all insufficient for predicting behaviour.
cards.use_when: When reviewing an innovation or marketing brief and deciding whether the framing is likely to predict customer choice.
steps: Audit the brief for the four default organising principles named in the source: product attributes, customer characteristics, trends, and competitive response.
Note these are not wrong, just insufficient: they describe who or what rather than why a choice happens.
Adding jobs as a lens means centring the circumstance rather than the customer segment or product category.
Rewrite your problem statement in terms of progress sought and obstacles faced, then check whether your existing data can answer it.
Use the answer to set the tradeoffs: which benefits are essential and which are extraneous to the new offering.
caveats: Jobs theory does not replace segmentation for execution purposes; it changes what the primary unit of innovation work is.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Learn from Toyota: design defects out with if-then process tests
cards.summary: Treating each defect as an anomaly to be root-caused and designed out of the process beat the Detroit approach of inspecting and reworking.
cards.use_when: When a repeatable process (fulfilment, creative production, onboarding) keeps producing errors that get patched rather than prevented.
steps: Stop defaulting to added inspection, inventory and rework, which the source says ballooned cost and complexity while leaving the root cause untouched.
Treat each defect as a scientist treats an anomaly: find its specific cause, then change the process so the error cannot recur.
Standardise each value-adding step: do it the same way every time, so that managers know whether the next step works with it.
See each standardised repetition as a test of the if-then statement: 'if we do this, then that will be the result.'
Accept that complexity (thousands of parts, hundreds of suppliers, many countries) does not make errors inevitable if the process focuses on identifying and removing causes.
caveats: The automotive quality story is used here as an analogy for innovation, not as an ecommerce case with measured results.
The source explicitly says innovation is still in a 'pre-quality revolution' state, so do not overstate how far this transfers.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Recognise the legacy process that produces what you don't want
cards.summary: US automakers unwittingly designed a process highly effective at producing costly, inconsistent cars - a warning about the systems behind your outcomes.
cards.use_when: When outcomes are consistently poor or unpredictable and the reflex is to add patching steps rather than redesign the process.
steps: Inventory the patches currently in place - extra checks, buffers, rework stages - and ask what problem each is mitigating rather than solving.
Ask what the current process is actually designed to produce, and whether that matches what you want customers to experience.
Reframe 'inherent randomness' as an untested assumption: the Japanese manufacturers showed that specific causes of defects existed and could be removed.
Shift investment from correction after the fact to prevention inside the process.
Expect quality and cost to improve together once root causes are removed, as happened with Japanese manufacturers in the 1970s and 1980s.
caveats: The historical account is descriptive; it does not guarantee the same cost trajectory in other industries.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Reframe a market by serving non-consumption
cards.summary: SNHU found its biggest opportunity not by beating local colleges but by serving adults who otherwise would have done nothing.
cards.use_when: When your category looks saturated and growth has stalled under a one-size-fits-all offer aimed at the 'average' customer.
steps: Identify the distinct jobs different groups hire you for, even when they look identical on paper (e.g. the same accounting degree for an 18-year-old and a 35-year-old).
For SNHU's coming-of-age students, the job centred on experiences - sports teams, climbing walls, long conversations with faculty - while parents asked about academics and financial aid.

For online adult learners, the job was different in kind: convenience, customer service, credentials and speedy completion, in the circumstance of juggling work and family with unfinished credits and debt.
Notice that the second group was also competing with non-consumption - doing nothing about their education - which makes the addressable market far larger than a local applicant pool.
Align policies, structures and service levels to the actual job; SNHU's financial-aid process was designed around a leisurely, low-urgency conversation that did not fit adult learners' needs.
caveats: SNHU's revenue growth figures (about $535m by fiscal 2016; 34% compounded annual growth over six years) are case results, not promises.
The source notes the online division earned a modest $32m before the reframing and succeeded somewhat despite, not because of, existing processes.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use a jobs lens to separate functional from experience-based buying
cards.summary: Prospects may ask about practical features while actually hiring you for a social and emotional experience, and the two require different offers.
cards.use_when: When designing a landing page, tour or sales conversation and deciding which elements actually drive the decision.
steps: Look at who asks which questions: in SNHU's case parents asked about academics and aid while prospective students asked about experiences.
Decide which dimension your core segment is really buying against, and build the offer and proof around it.
If the buying dimension is experiential, the functional questions still need answering but are not the primary persuasive content.
Consider serving both dimensions with differentiated journeys rather than one generic pitch for the 'average' customer.
Treat a generic message as a warning sign that you have not distinguished the jobs your different customers are hiring you for.
caveats: This is a qualitative read from one university example; verify with your own prospect conversations before rebuilding a funnel.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Map competition as a shifted landscape, not a finite share fight
cards.summary: Seeing competition through jobs changes who you benchmark and how you innovate, from supply-side selling to demand-side responding.
cards.use_when: When your strategic plan assumes growth must come from taking share from direct rivals in a fixed market.
steps: List every alternative a customer might choose for the job, including products from other categories and doing nothing.
Accept that some competitors are invisible at first: Reid Hoffman's point that 'sometimes it's a job you can't currently see.'
Watch for incumbents redefining themselves around jobs, as Ford described itself as a mobility company and GM invested in Lyft and launched Maven.
Shift from a supply-side view (what we make, dealers as customers) to a demand-side view (what job the buyer is trying to get done).
Expect competitive advantage to go to whoever understands and best solves the job, including the surrounding experiences and removing roadblocks to progress.
caveats: Strategic repositioning examples from BMW, Ford and GM are illustrations from the source, not verified outcomes for ecommerce.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Accept that the job endures while solutions change
cards.summary: Jobs are discovered, not created, and the underlying job stays stable even as the way people solve it changes dramatically.
cards.use_when: When evaluating a new technology or channel and wondering whether it changes the customer's need or just the means of solving it.
steps: Ask what enduring job your category solves - sharing information across distances persisted from Pony Express to email.
Teenagers' job of communicating without parental oversight persisted from passing notes to Snapchat, which solved it with disappearing messages.
Focus on understanding the underlying job rather than falling in love with your current solution, because a better solution can always displace yours.

Keep improving your understanding of the complex social, emotional and functional needs in each circumstance - the source says Snapchat itself remains vulnerable to someone with a better understanding.
caveats: Don't read this as an argument to ignore new technology; the source says new technology can improve how a job is solved.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Convert jobs insight into experience and process requirements
cards.summary: A layered job usually cannot be satisfied by a product alone; it demands a bundle of integrated experiences, which is where defensibility comes from.
cards.use_when: When moving from research findings to designing the full customer experience, including post-purchase and service layers.
steps: List every dimension of the job - functional, social and emotional - and the tradeoffs the customer said they would make.
Design an experience that addresses each dimension, not just the core functional transaction.
Integrate those experiences into company processes so they are delivered consistently rather than as isolated campaigns.
Treat the integration as the moat: the source argues that when you have done this well it is almost impossible for competitors to copy.
Test each element against the job rather than against competitor feature lists.
caveats: This is a claim about defensibility from the authors; it assumes deep integration, not a single added feature.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Run leadership questions to test customer understanding
cards.summary: A short question set checks whether you actually know why customers choose you and who you are really competing with.
cards.use_when: When preparing a strategy review, onboarding a team, or stress-testing a positioning statement.
steps: Ask: do you understand the real reason customers choose your product, or why they choose something else instead?
Ask how your product helps customers make progress and in which circumstances they are trying to make it.
Break the progress into functional, emotional and social dimensions and record what you know versus what you are assuming.
Ask what else is competing for that job, including options outside the traditional view of your industry and non-consumption.
Close the gaps with direct customer research where answers are weak or generic.
caveats: These are diagnostic prompts, not a measurement instrument; pair them with evidence from customers.
